prompt:
A 63-year-old man with a remote history of rectal cancer and multiple prior small-bowel obstructions was hospitalized a few weeks ago for community-acquired pneumonia. CT chest at that time showed predominantly peripheral multilobar consolidations and ground-glass opacities. He completed intravenous antibiotics, was weaned off oxygen within 2 weeks, and discharged home. At his discharge follow-up he remained fatigued with persistent leukocytosis, a new anemia (hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL from 10.7 g/dL at discharge), and marked peripheral eosinophilia (>3.4 × 10^3/uL). I empirically started prednisone 60 mg daily for eosinophilic pneumonia. Is bronchoscopy required to confirm the diagnosis?

Provide a comprehensive management plan including appropriate diagnostic workup, referrals, procedures if indicated, follow-up, and actions to avoid.

rubric_items.text: Order Strongyloides stercoralis IgG serology before or promptly after starting high-dose corticosteroids.
Obtain stool ova and parasite examinations when epidemiologic exposure suggests a parasitic infection.
Review recent medications and exposures for a potential cause of drug-induced eosinophilic lung disease.
Order ANCA testing with MPO and PR3 antibodies to evaluate for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
Assess for extrapulmonary eosinophilic disease, including rash, neuropathy, sinus disease, renal abnormalities, and cardiac symptoms.
Order HIV antigen/antibody testing.
Order Aspergillus-specific IgE and IgG testing if asthma, bronchiectasis, or another feature of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is present.
Repeat a CBC with differential within one week to trend eosinophilia, leukocytosis, and anemia.
Obtain a reticulocyte count, iron studies, ferritin, and peripheral smear to evaluate the new anemia.
Order a comprehensive metabolic panel to assess renal, hepatic, and steroid-related metabolic abnormalities.
Order troponin and BNP to screen for eosinophil-associated cardiac involvement.
Refer the patient to pulmonology for evaluation of suspected eosinophilic pneumonia and supervision of corticosteroid treatment.
Obtain pulmonary function testing with DLCO after the acute illness stabilizes.
Defer routine bronchoscopy when the compatible CT pattern, marked peripheral eosinophilia, and clinical course adequately support the diagnosis.
Perform bronchoscopy with BAL if the diagnosis remains uncertain, the patient deteriorates, treatment response is inadequate, or an opportunistic infection must be excluded.
Continue systemic corticosteroids at an appropriate initial dose if still indicated after reassessment, with a supervised taper guided by clinical and radiographic response.
Arrange follow-up within one to two weeks to reassess symptoms, oxygenation, laboratory results, and corticosteroid response.

Arrange follow-up chest imaging in approximately four to eight weeks to document improvement or resolution, using chest radiography when sufficient and CT when abnormalities persist, are atypical, or require further characterization.
Counsel the patient about corticosteroid adverse effects, hyperglycemia, and signs of opportunistic infection.
Counsel the patient about the risk of Strongyloides hyperinfection during high-dose corticosteroid therapy.
Provide calcium and vitamin D supplementation if a prolonged corticosteroid course is anticipated.

Provide Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis, usually trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole if not contraindicated, when the anticipated corticosteroid dose and duration together with patient-specific risk meet an accepted prophylaxis guideline.
Arrange colonoscopy if iron deficiency is identified or colorectal cancer surveillance is overdue.
Refer to hematology if marked eosinophilia persists despite treatment or if smear abnormalities or other evidence of a clonal disorder emerges.
Declare eosinophilic pneumonia definitively confirmed and all secondary causes excluded without completing an etiologic evaluation.
Continue prolonged high-dose corticosteroids without screening for Strongyloides infection.
Abruptly discontinue prednisone without a taper after prolonged systemic exposure (three to four weeks or more) that carries adrenal-suppression risk.
Continue high-dose prednisone indefinitely without a response assessment or taper plan.
Prescribe additional broad-spectrum antibiotics solely for persistent leukocytosis without evidence of ongoing bacterial infection.
Rechallenge the patient with a recently administered medication suspected of causing eosinophilia.
Perform an immediate bone marrow biopsy before reassessing the eosinophilia and evaluating common secondary causes.
Initiate an anti-IL-5 biologic as first-line treatment for this presentation.
Initiate cyclophosphamide without evidence of eosinophilic vasculitis or another established indication.
Transfuse packed red blood cells solely for a stable hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL.
Use inhaled corticosteroid monotherapy to treat the current eosinophilic pneumonia.
Order chest CT scans every one to two weeks for routine monitoring.
Advise the patient to ignore worsening dyspnea, fever, hemoptysis, chest pain, or hypoxemia.
Discharge the patient from follow-up without arranging reassessment of eosinophilia, anemia, and pulmonary infiltrates.
Treat with ivermectin if Strongyloides testing is positive, or empirically with infectious-disease guidance when exposure risk is substantial and high-dose corticosteroids cannot await results.
